subject: Chemistry
title: How Baking Soda Makes Cakes Rise
description: One-minute skill: How Baking Soda Makes Cakes Rise.

hook.text: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate. When it meets acid, it produces CO₂ gas—and your cake rises.

buildup.text: Recipes pair baking soda with buttermilk, lemon juice, or vinegar. All are acids.

discovery.text: The acid-base reaction releases carbon dioxide bubbles. They get trapped in batter and expand when heated.

twist.text: Baking powder already contains both the base and a dry acid. Just add water and it activates.

climax.text: Double-acting baking powder reacts twice: once when wet, again when heated. That's the secret to fluffy cakes.

punchline.text: Acid meets base, gas escapes, batter rises. Chemistry bakes your cake.

quiz.question: What gas makes cakes rise when baking soda reacts with acid?

details.summary: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate that reacts with acids in batter to produce carbon dioxide gas. The gas forms tiny bubbles that expand during baking, creating the light and fluffy texture of cakes and breads..
details.whyItMatters: Baking chemistry demonstrates acid-base reactions and gas production in an everyday context. Understanding leavening agents explains why recipes require specific ingredient ratios.
takeaways: Baking soda reacts with acids to produce carbon dioxide bubbles
Baking powder contains both the base and an acid for self-leavening
Double-acting baking powder reacts twice—when mixed and when heated

faq.question: What happens if you use too much baking soda in a recipe?
faq.answer: Excess baking soda that does not react with acid remains in the batter and gives the finished product a bitter, soapy taste. It can also cause the batter to rise too rapidly and then collapse, creating a dense texture. Precise measurement matters in baking chemistry.

faq.question: Why does baking powder contain cream of tartar?
faq.answer: Cream of tartar is an acid salt (potassium bitartrate) that reacts with sodium bicarbonate when dissolved in liquid. Including the acid in the powder means the recipe does not need an acidic ingredient like buttermilk or yogurt to trigger the carbon dioxide reaction.
